name: Cognitive Rehabilitation
title: Cognitive Rehabilitation
answer: Cognitive rehabilitation covers the therapies, exercises and assistive tools used to help people recover or compensate for changes in attention, memory, language and executive function after injury or illness. It sits inside neuroinformatics and the brain because much of the work now involves software that tracks performance, adapts difficulty and models how a person's cognition changes over time. The field spans stroke and traumatic brain injury recovery, progressive conditions such as dementia, and developmental needs, and it overlaps with neurology, speech and language therapy, occupational therapy and neuropsychology.

crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

sections.body: Cognitive rehabilitation covers the therapies, exercises and assistive tools used to help people recover or compensate for changes in attention, memory, language and executive function after injury or illness. It sits inside neuroinformatics and the brain because much of the work now involves software that tracks performance, adapts difficulty and models how a person's cognition changes over time. The field spans stroke and traumatic brain injury recovery, progressive conditions such as dementia, and developmental needs, and it overlaps with neurology, speech and language therapy, occupational therapy and neuropsychology.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The technical base is usually a mix of consumer devices and clinical systems. Tablets and phones run most patient facing exercises, wearables and sensors capture activity and sleep, and clinicians work from electronic health records and specialised cognitive testing platforms. Behind these sit data pipelines that store repeated test scores, reaction times and imaging or electrophysiology where available, plus the statistical and machine learning models that score performance and adjust task difficulty. Cloud hosting, secure identity management and interoperability standards such as FHIR matter because these tools often need to exchange data with hospital records.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: Work typically begins with a baseline assessment using validated neuropsychological tests, then moves to a plan of repeated practice with feedback. Digital versions automate scoring, vary item difficulty in response to accuracy and speed, and log every session so progress can be charted. Machine learning is used to detect patterns in that longitudinal data, to predict who is likely to plateau or decline, and to personalise the next task. Clinicians review the output, adjust goals and decide when a compensatory strategy or a assistive device is more useful than further drill.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Cognitive rehabilitation data is sensitive health information, so consent, data protection rules and clinical validation all apply. Software that claims a diagnostic or therapeutic purpose may be regulated as a medical device, which brings requirements for evidence, labelling and post market surveillance. Provenance matters because a model trained on one patient group may not transfer to another, and clinicians need to know what data and assumptions sit behind a score.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The direction of travel is toward continuous, home based monitoring that supplements clinic visits, with models that adapt in real time and flag meaningful change to a care team. Better speech, vision and wearable sensing should widen what can be measured outside a testing room, and shared data standards should make it easier to compare tools across sites. The open questions are clinical: which digital measures actually predict real world function, how to keep a person's own goals central, and how to show benefit in trials rather than only in engagement metrics.
